term:Activation Function.deep_dive:
An activation function is applied to the weighted sum of a neuron's inputs and produces the neuron's output; it is typically nonlinear. The nonlinearity is the whole point: without it, a stack of layers would collapse into a single linear transformation, and the network could not represent the complex, curved decision boundaries that make deep learning useful. ISO/IEC 22989 gives threshold, sigmoid and polynomial functions as examples; in practice ReLU and its variants dominate.

The governance relevance is indirect but real. The choice of activation function is a design decision made during Design & Construction, it shapes how the model behaves and how it can fail, and it is one of the architectural features that must be documented for reproducibility and audit. Because activation functions make the model nonlinear, they are part of the reason a trained network's behaviour cannot be read off from its weights: the function is applied at every neuron, across many layers, and the composition is what resists interpretation.

The exam angle is conceptual: an activation function is the nonlinear step inside a neuron that lets a network learn complex features. It is a building block of the connectionist architecture, not a governance instrument, but it helps explain why deep networks are opaque.
term:Activation Function.exam_tip: Activation function: the typically nonlinear function applied to a neuron's weighted inputs, the reason a network can learn complex features and the reason its weights alone explain nothing. ISO 22989 examples are threshold, sigmoid and polynomial.

term:Accountability.deep_dive:
Accountability is the state of being answerable for actions, decisions and performance. ISO/IEC 22989 is precise: it is an assigned responsibility, based on regulation, agreement or delegation, owed to another party using specified means and criteria. That structure matters: accountability is not a feeling of responsibility, it is a relationship with a named party who can hold you to account, by defined means, against defined criteria.

The legal backbone is GDPR Article 5(2), which makes the controller responsible for, and able to demonstrate, compliance with the data protection principles. EU AI Act Article 16 places the provider under obligations it must be able to evidence, and the NIST AI RMF makes **accountable and transparent** one of its trustworthiness characteristics, the one that makes the rest enforceable rather than aspirational. ISO/IEC 42001 embeds accountability through defined roles, responsibilities and authorities in the AI management system.

The distinction the exam tests: accountability is who answers for the outcome; responsibility is who performs the work. You can delegate tasks but not the answerability, and it must attach to a named human or organisation. "The algorithm decided" is exactly the failure mode accountability frameworks exist to prevent.
term:Accountability.exam_tip: Accountability is being answerable to a named party by specified means, not just doing the work (that is responsibility). GDPR Article 5(2) makes it demonstrable; NIST calls it the characteristic that makes the others enforceable; it must land on a named human.

ref_22989.overview: ISO/IEC 22989:2022 is the AI terminology standard: more than 110 defined concepts covering the AI lifecycle, machine learning paradigms, system roles (AI provider, manufacturer, customer, subject) and trustworthiness properties. It defines, and does not prescribe. It is the vocabulary that other ISO AI standards and regulators lean on, and it is free from the IEC webstore.
ref_22989.deep_dive:
### What it is

ISO/IEC 22989, Information technology, Artificial intelligence, Artificial intelligence concepts and terminology, was published in 2022 by ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42. Its job is terminological: to give everyone the same words, not to tell anyone how to run a program. That is why the BOK names it first among the core ISO standards. 42001 and 23894 both build on its vocabulary, and the trustworthiness properties it defines reappear across the EU AI Act and the NIST AI RMF.

### AI the discipline, AI system the artifact

The standard's sharpest distinction is between **AI** and an **AI system**. AI is defined as a discipline, the research and development of mechanisms and applications, and the context note describes a technical and scientific field dealing with systems that generate outputs such as content, predictions, recommendations or decisions for a specific, human-defined objective. An **AI system** is the engineered artifact: a technical system that generates those results, using techniques that build a model of data, knowledge or processes, and designed to operate with varying degrees of automation. Keeping the two apart avoids the common error of treating "AI" as a thing you can buy.

### The roles

22989 supplies a role taxonomy the other standards use: **AI provider** (makes the system available), **AI manufacturer** (builds or assembles it), **AI customer** (acquires it), **AI partner** (collaborates), and **AI subject** (the person affected by or interacting with it). These are not the EU AI Act's provider, deployer, importer and distributor, so map them carefully rather than treating them as synonyms.

### The trustworthiness vocabulary

This is the cluster the exam tests most. The standard defines **trustworthiness** as the ability to meet the expectations of interested parties in a verifiable manner, and lists the characteristics that make it up: reliability, availability, resilience, security, privacy, accountability, transparency, integrity, authenticity, quality and user-friendliness. The pairs that trip people up:

- **Robustness** (maintain performance under all circumstances) versus **resilience** (recover operational state after an incident).
- **Reliability** (intended behaviour and results correspond) versus **accuracy**.
- **Verification** (did we build the system right, against its specifications) versus **validation** (did we build the right system, fit for its intended use).
- **Explainability** (why this output) versus **transparency** (information about the system made available).

### Lifecycle and learning

22989 sets out an AI system life cycle: adoption and requirements, design and construction, verification and validation, deployment, operation and monitoring, continuous validation, reassessment and decommissioning. It also defines the learning paradigms (supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, reinforcement, transfer learning) and the symbolic, subsymbolic and hybrid approaches. 42001 and 23894 both reference the life cycle.

### Why it matters

It is the lexicon. When a question hinges on the precise meaning of an AI concept, 22989 is the source being quoted, and it is free: the IEC webstore publishes it at no charge, which makes it the one core ISO AI standard a candidate can actually read.
ref_22989.exam: The definitions themselves are the test material, and many flashcards trace here. Precision matters: robustness (performance under all circumstances) versus resilience (recovery), reliability versus accuracy, verification (built right) versus validation (right system). Know the role taxonomy and the lifecycle stages. Because 22989 is free from the IEC webstore, an item can quote its wording directly, so read the definitions rather than paraphrasing them.
key_points: The shared vocabulary standard: more than 110 terms that 42001, 23894 and others normatively reference
AI is defined as a discipline; the AI system is the engineered artifact that generates content, predictions, recommendations or decisions for a human-defined objective
Role taxonomy: AI provider, AI manufacturer, AI customer, AI partner, AI subject (distinct from the EU AI Act's provider, deployer, importer and distributor)
Trustworthiness vocabulary: robustness, reliability, resilience, controllability, predictability, transparency, explainability, accountability, availability
Verification checks specifications (built right); validation checks fitness for intended use (built the right system)
Lifecycle model: adoption, design and construction, verification and validation, deployment, operation and monitoring, continuous validation, reassessment, decommissioning
Learning taxonomy: supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, reinforcement and transfer learning, with symbolic, subsymbolic and hybrid approaches
Free from the IEC webstore, which makes it the most readable of the core ISO AI standards

ref_oecd.overview: The OECD Recommendation on Artificial Intelligence (OECD/LEGAL/0449), adopted 22 May 2019, was the first intergovernmental AI standard. The OECD Council revised its AI system definition on 8 November 2023 and the Recommendation more broadly on 3 May 2024. Five values-based principles and five recommendations to policy makers sit alongside working tools: a classification framework, incident and hazard definitions, and the Hiroshima reporting framework.
ref_oecd.deep_dive:
### The Recommendation

Adopted **22 May 2019** as the first intergovernmental AI standard, and revised in 2023 and 2024. It is **not binding**: adherents (47 as of September 2026, the EU among them) make a political commitment to implement it. At the June 2019 Osaka Summit, G20 leaders welcomed G20 AI Principles drawn from it.

### The five principles (2024 headings)

1. **Inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being** - beneficial outcomes for people and the planet, augmenting human capabilities, reducing inequalities, environmental sustainability (explicit since 2024).
2. **Respect for the rule of law, human rights and democratic values, including fairness and privacy** - non-discrimination, dignity, autonomy, privacy, labour rights, and safeguards against AI-amplified mis- and disinformation (the 2019 heading was "human-centred values and fairness").
3. **Transparency and explainability** - meaningful information on capabilities and limits, awareness of AI interactions, plain-language information on the factors and logic, and enough information for adversely affected people to challenge outputs.
4. **Robustness, security and safety** - function under normal use, foreseeable misuse and adverse conditions, with mechanisms to override, repair or decommission safely.
5. **Accountability** - role-based accountability, traceability of datasets, processes and decisions, and systematic risk management across the lifecycle.

### The five recommendations to policy makers

Invest in AI R&D; foster an inclusive AI-enabling ecosystem; shape an enabling interoperable governance and policy environment; build human capacity and prepare for labour-market transformation; and co-operate internationally for trustworthy AI.

### The 2023 definition update

The current AI system definition: a machine-based system that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers from the input it receives how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments, with systems varying in autonomy and adaptiveness after deployment. The five edits were "explicit or implicit" objectives, inference from the input, "content" added to the outputs, "physical" replacing "real", and adaptiveness after deployment. The EU AI Act's Article 3(1) closely tracks this wording.

### The May 2024 revision

New language on information integrity (AI-amplified mis- and disinformation, with respect for freedom of expression), coverage of use outside the intended purpose and of intentional and unintentional misuse, clearer transparency and responsible-disclosure guidance, safe override and decommissioning, responsible business conduct across the lifecycle, interoperable governance across jurisdictions, and an explicit reference to environmental sustainability. There are still five principles.

### The tools

The **Framework for the Classification of AI Systems** (February 2022) has five dimensions: People and Planet, Economic Context, Data and Input, AI Model, and Task and Output; **action autonomy** is a Task and Output criterion, not an AI Model one. The **incident and hazard definitions** (May 2024) separate an AI incident (realised harm) from an AI hazard (an event that could plausibly lead to one, with near misses counting). The **AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor (AIM)** tracks publicly reported events, and the **Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework** (OECD-hosted since February 2025) lets organizations report against the G7 Code of Conduct in a common format.
ref_oecd.exam: BOK v2.1 II.D covers the OECD's principles, framework, policies and recommended practices, so study the tools as well as the list. Know the five principles by their 2024 headings, the five definition edits, the five classification dimensions (with action autonomy as a Task and Output criterion), and incident versus hazard. Dates: adopted 22 May 2019, definition revised 8 November 2023, broader revision 3 May 2024. Remember it is a non-binding Recommendation.

ref_nist_rmf.overview: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (January 2023): the US government's voluntary, sector-agnostic framework for managing AI risk. Four core functions (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) run around seven trustworthiness characteristics (valid and reliable; safe; secure and resilient; accountable and transparent; explainable and interpretable; privacy-enhanced; fair with harmful bias managed). It is not certifiable, and profiles tailor it to specific settings.
ref_nist_rmf.deep_dive:
### What it is

Published January 2023, directed by Congress and built through open consultation. It is voluntary, rights-preserving and sector-agnostic, and it is a framework rather than a standard: there is no certification. It was accompanied by the AI RMF Playbook and, in July 2024, the Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1).

### What makes AI risk unique

AI risk is **contextual** (the same system is high-risk in one deployment and low-risk in another), **emergent** (outcomes unintended or unforeseen at design time), tied to **opacity** (adaptive algorithms produce unpredictable results), **societal in scale** (outputs reach millions instantly), and **data-driven** (risks come from biased data, proxies or deployment context). The framework also names two kinds of uncertainty: **epistemic** (unknowns from limited knowledge, such as insufficient training data) and **aleatoric** (inherent randomness, such as sensor noise).

### The four functions

| Function | Job |
|---|---|
| **GOVERN** | The cross-cutting foundation: policies, processes and procedures; roles and responsibilities (including oversight bodies and escalation); risk tolerance and appetite; and an organizational culture that lets people raise concerns |
| **MAP** | Understand context: intended purpose and foreseeable misuse, system design and data, stakeholders and affected populations, and prioritised risks with their uncertainty |
| **MEASURE** | Assess: metrics and indicators, evaluation methods (testing, red teaming, stress testing, expert panels, third-party audits), performance monitoring, and risk documentation |
| **MANAGE** | Respond: risk treatment (accept, transfer, avoid, mitigate), incident response and recovery, integration with cybersecurity, privacy and enterprise risk, and risk evolution and system retirement |

GOVERN is the most relevant function for an AI governance professional, because it is where culture, accountability and appetite are set. Performance is not trustworthiness: a highly accurate model can still encode harmful stereotypes or erode autonomy, which is why MAP requires qualitative context, not just metrics.

### The seven trustworthiness characteristics

Valid and reliable; safe; secure and resilient; accountable and transparent; explainable and interpretable; privacy-enhanced; and fair with harmful bias managed. They are the yardstick MEASURE works against.

### Profiles and the CSF contrast

A **profile** implements the RMF for a specific setting, technology or sector; the Generative AI Profile is the flagship example. Compared with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the AI RMF treats risk as emergent, systemic and value-laden rather than a set of known threats to defend against with controls; explainability, fairness and ethical dimensions are core rather than out of scope.
ref_nist_rmf.exam: The four functions and seven trustworthiness characteristics are heavily tested, so memorise both lists. Know which function does what: GOVERN is culture, policy, roles and appetite; MAP is context and risk identification; MEASURE is evaluation and monitoring; MANAGE is treatment and incident response. Trustworthy AI is valid and reliable; safe; secure and resilient; accountable and transparent; explainable and interpretable; privacy-enhanced; fair with harmful bias managed. Remember the RMF is voluntary and non-certifiable, and that profiles tailor it.

ref_playbook.overview: The NIST AI RMF Playbook is the practical companion to the AI RMF: suggested actions, documentation prompts and references for every one of the framework's 72 subcategories, organised under the four functions. The BOK names it directly, so it is exam material rather than background, and it is the place to look when a question asks what an organization should actually do.
ref_playbook.deep_dive:
### What it is

The AI RMF sets out functions, categories and subcategories. The Playbook takes each subcategory and supplies what to do about it: **suggested actions** (concrete steps an organization can take), **transparency and documentation prompts** (what to record so the work is auditable), and **references** (the standards and guidance behind the action). It is not a separate framework; it is the RMF's how-to layer, and NIST has said a revision will follow the AI RMF 1.0 update.

### How it is organised

| Layer | Example |
|---|---|
| Function | GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE |
| Category | e.g. GOVERN 1, "Policies, processes, procedures and practices" |
| Subcategory | e.g. GOVERN 1.1, legal and regulatory requirements are understood and managed |
| Playbook entry | Suggested actions, documentation prompts and references for that subcategory |

The subcategories carry the framework's normative content, and the Playbook is where a governance team turns them into a work plan. Because the actions are suggestions rather than requirements, an organization can adopt, adapt or document why it chose otherwise, which is exactly the kind of evidence an auditor or a regulator wants to see.

### AI actors

The Playbook and the RMF use **AI actors**: the people and organizations playing a role in the lifecycle, from those who design and build, through those who deploy and operate, to those affected and those who oversee. Naming the actor matters because the same subcategory can land on different teams, and because governance has to reach everyone who touches the system rather than only the builders.

### How to use it

Read the Playbook alongside the framework: the framework tells you what the risk process must contain, and the Playbook tells you what a reasonable organization does about each piece. In an exam item that asks which instrument supplies practical, per-subcategory guidance for the NIST framework, the answer is the Playbook; if the question asks for the risk process itself, it is the AI RMF; and if it asks about generative AI specifically, it is NIST AI 600-1.
ref_playbook.exam: Know what the Playbook is for: per-subcategory suggested actions, documentation prompts and references, under the four functions. A matching question may contrast it with the AI RMF (the framework itself) and with AI 600-1 (the generative AI profile). Remember the subcategory numbering convention (function, then category, then subcategory, such as GOVERN 1.1) and that the actions are suggestions, not requirements.

ref_600.overview: NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024) is the Generative AI Profile: a cross-sectoral profile that applies the AI RMF to generative AI. It defines 12 risks that generative AI creates or worsens, organises suggested actions under the four RMF functions, and adds four primary considerations (governance, pre-deployment testing, content provenance, incident disclosure). It was developed under Executive Order 14110.
ref_600.deep_dive:
### What it is

A **profile** implements the AI RMF's functions, categories and subcategories for a specific setting, technology or sector. AI 600-1 is the cross-sectoral profile for generative AI, published July 2024 pursuant to Executive Order 14110 on Safe, Secure and Trustworthy AI. It does not replace the AI RMF; it tailors it.

### The 12 generative AI risks

CBRN information or capabilities; **confabulation** (confidently stated false content, colloquially "hallucination"); dangerous, violent or hateful content; data privacy (leakage, memorisation, inference and de-anonymisation); environmental impacts; harmful bias and homogenisation; human-AI configuration (anthropomorphisation, algorithmic aversion, automation bias, over-reliance, emotional entanglement); information integrity (misinformation and disinformation); information security (prompt injection, data poisoning, offensive cyber capability); intellectual property; obscene, degrading or abusive content including non-consensual intimate imagery and CSAM; and value chain and component integration.

They are often grouped three ways: technical or model risks (malfunction), misuse by humans (malicious), and ecosystem or societal risks (systemic).

### Four primary considerations

1. **Governance** - organizational structures, policies and third-party oversight.
2. **Pre-deployment testing** - TEVV (testing, evaluation, verification and validation) before release.
3. **Content provenance** - tracking the origin and history of digital content, so synthetic material can be identified.
4. **Incident disclosure** - reporting, documenting and sharing incident information.

### Why it matters

The profile is where the AI RMF's abstractions become generative-AI specifics. Two examples the exam can use: **confabulation** is the formal term for hallucination, and it is dangerous because fabricated citations and reasoning mislead users into inappropriate trust; and **automation bias** (excessive deference to the system) is a human-AI configuration risk that amplifies confabulation and bias. **Content provenance** is the concept behind watermarking and labelling duties such as the EU AI Act's Article 50 marking.

### Relationship to the other instruments

AI 600-1 sits under the AI RMF as a profile, and its suggested actions are organised by the same subcategories as the Playbook. The Texas TRAIGA defences expressly recognise substantial compliance with the NIST AI RMF Generative AI Profile, which is a concrete example of a voluntary framework carrying legal weight.
ref_600.exam: Know that AI 600-1 is the Generative AI Profile, developed under Executive Order 14110, and that it defines 12 generative-AI risks. Confabulation is the formal term for hallucination, and content provenance is the concept behind watermarking and labelling. The four primary considerations are governance, pre-deployment testing, content provenance and incident disclosure. A profile tailors the RMF; it does not replace it.

ref_42001.overview: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is the world's first certifiable AI management system (AIMS) standard, published December 2023. Built on the Annex SL high-level structure and the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle, and modelled on ISO 27001 and ISO 9001, it is the standard an organization certifies against to show it governs AI systematically. Impact assessment is a requirement, not an option.
ref_42001.deep_dive:
### What it is

Published **December 2023** (first edition), and still current as of September 2026 with no amendment or revision listed. It specifies requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an AI management system. It is **certifiable**, which is what separates it from 22989 (terminology), 42005 (impact assessment guidance) and 23894 (risk guidance). It scales from a startup to a multinational, and it is modelled on ISO 27001 (information security) and ISO 9001 (quality).

### Structure

Annex SL gives it the common clause layout: context of the organization (internal and external factors, applicable laws and standards), leadership and commitment, planning (risk assessment, objectives, trustworthiness goals), support (resources, competence, awareness, documentation), operation (design, acquisition, development, deployment), performance evaluation (monitoring, audit, management review), and improvement (corrective action, continual improvement). The Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle runs through it.

### Impact assessment is required

Clause **6.1.4** (planning) has the organization define an AI system impact assessment process, and clause **8.4** (operation) has it perform those assessments at planned intervals or when significant changes are proposed. Normative Annex A objective **A.5**, "Assessing impacts of AI systems", adds controls on the process (A.5.2), its documentation (A.5.3), impacts on individuals or groups (A.5.4) and societal impacts (A.5.5). ISO/IEC 42005 is the companion guidance on how to do it. This is the point most likely to be tested: 42001 requires the assessment; 42005 explains how.

### Trustworthiness dimensions

The standard requires consideration of transparency and explainability, fairness and non-discrimination, robustness and resilience, accountability and human oversight, and privacy and data governance.

### Implementation

Four steps recur in practice: a readiness or gap assessment (inventory the AI systems, policies, roles and documentation); integration with existing management systems (27001, 9001, 27701, sharing risk registers, incident response and audit functions); AI-specific policies (lifecycle management, ethical principles, bias detection and mitigation, monitoring, stakeholder engagement); and training so technical staff understand the obligations and business users escalate AI risks.

### Who certifies

ISO/IEC 42006:2025 sets requirements, additional to ISO/IEC 17021-1, for the bodies that audit and certify against 42001. It regulates the certifiers, not the certified organization, which is why it is a favourite distractor: 42001 is the AIMS you certify, 42005 is impact-assessment guidance, and 42006 is the rules for whoever issues the 42001 certificate.
ref_42001.exam: The reliable items are structural: 42001 is the certifiable AI management system, published December 2023, built on Annex SL and PDCA, modelled on ISO 27001. Impact assessment is a requirement (6.1.4, 8.4, Annex A.5), and 42005 is the how-to companion. Do not confuse 42001 with 42005 (guidance, not certifiable) or 42006 (rules for certification bodies). Know the trustworthiness dimensions it requires.

ref_42005.overview: ISO/IEC 42005:2025 (published 28 May 2025) is guidance on AI system impact assessment: how and when to assess the impacts an AI system and its foreseeable applications can have on individuals, groups and societies, what to document, and how to integrate the work with AI risk management and an AI management system. It is guidance, not certifiable, and it is one of the BOK's core three.
ref_42005.deep_dive:
### What it is

Published **28 May 2025** (first edition, 39 pages) by ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42. It is for any organization that develops, provides or uses AI, of any size. It is **guidance, not certifiable**: it tells you how to do an impact assessment, while 42001 requires that you do one. It is one of exactly three core ISO standards in BOK v2.1, alongside 22989 and 42001.

### Clause 5: the process

The process covers documenting it, integrating it with other management processes, timing, scope, allocating responsibilities, thresholds for sensitive uses, restricted uses and impact scales, performing it, analysing the results, recording and reporting, approval, and monitoring and review. Two points matter: it is **lifecycle, not one-off** (assess at design and before deployment, keep it under review, and reassess when intended use, the system or the legal and policy context changes significantly), and it is **two-sided** (benefits and harms both belong in the record, each with measures).

### Clause 6: the record

The record covers the scope; system information (description, capabilities, purpose, intended and unintended uses); data and data quality; algorithms and models; the deployment environment (geography, languages, constraints); interested parties; actual and reasonably foreseeable benefits and harms, including failures and misuse; and measures.

### The annexes

Informative annexes cover use with 42001 (A), use with 23894 (B), a harms and benefits taxonomy (C), aligning with other assessments (D), and an example template (E). Annex B is the bridge to risk management: it explains how impact findings feed a 23894-style risk process.

### Relationship to law and to the other standards

An impact assessment can feed a GDPR Article 35 DPIA or an EU AI Act Article 27 fundamental rights impact assessment, but it **replaces neither**, and because 42005 is not a harmonised standard it gives no presumption of conformity under the AI Act. The split to remember: **42005 asks about impacts on people; 23894 asks about risk to the organization.** 42001 requires the assessment; 42005 explains how; 42006 covers the certifiers.

### The reassessment trigger

A reassessment is triggered by a change in intended use, a significant system change (data or model), or a new legal or policy requirement. That trigger is a favourite exam detail because it captures the lifecycle idea: an impact assessment is a living record, not a document filed once.
ref_42005.exam: Match the standard to the job: 42005 is AI system impact assessment guidance, published May 2025, guidance rather than certifiable, and one of the BOK's core three. Reassessment triggers are a favourite detail: changed intended use, a significant system change, or a new legal or policy requirement. Do not confuse it with 42001 (which requires the assessment) or 23894 (risk to the organization).

ref_23894.overview: ISO/IEC 23894:2023 is AI-specific risk management guidance, extending the ISO 31000 risk-management approach to AI. It is background only in BOK v2.1, which names just three core ISO standards (22989, 42001 and 42005), but it remains the reference point for the AI risk process and 42005's Annex B maps impact findings into it.
ref_23894.deep_dive:
### What it is

Published **2023**, ISO/IEC 23894 gives guidance on managing risk related to AI, built on the **ISO 31000** risk-management framework (the general standard whose definition of risk is "the effect of uncertainty on objectives"). It is guidance, not certifiable. Its focus is risk management **of** AI, not using AI to do risk management, which is a distinction the standard is careful to draw.

### What it adds to ISO 31000

ISO 31000 supplies the generic process: establish context, identify, analyse, evaluate, treat, monitor and review, with communication and consultation throughout. 23894 carries that process into AI's specifics: the risk sources particular to AI, how the process maps onto the AI system lifecycle, and the governance and accountability arrangements needed for AI risk. Its Annex B sets out AI risk sources, and Annex C maps risk management processes to the lifecycle (inception, design and development, verification and validation, deployment, operation and monitoring, retirement).

### How it relates to the others

It complements 42001: 42001 is the certifiable management system that holds risk management as one of its processes, and 23894 is the detailed guidance on the risk process itself. It also connects to 42005: Annex B of 42005 explains how the findings of an impact assessment feed a 23894-style risk process. The line to keep straight is the direction of the question: **23894 asks about risk to the organization; 42005 asks about impacts on people.** A governance program usually wants both, because a system that harms people harms the organization too, but the two standards answer different questions and feed different records.

### BOK status

Not named in BOK v2.1 II.D, which lists 22989, 42001 and 42005 as a closed set, and not named in v2.0.1 either. Recognize it as useful background and as a distractor: an item that asks which ISO standard covers AI risk management may be looking for 23894, but an item that asks which are the BOK's core three is looking for the other list.
ref_23894.exam: Know 23894 as AI risk-management guidance extending ISO 31000, guidance rather than certifiable, and background only in BOK v2.1. The tested distinction is 23894 (risk to the organization) versus 42005 (impacts on people), and 23894 (detailed risk process guidance) versus 42001 (the certifiable management system that contains a risk process). Do not include it in the core three, which are 22989, 42001 and 42005.

term:General Data Protection Regulation.deep_dive:
Regulation (EU) 2016/679 is the EU's comprehensive data protection law. It entered into force on 24 May 2016 and applied from 25 May 2018. It governs the processing of personal data of people in the EU, and Article 3 gives it extraterritorial reach: it binds controllers and processors outside the EU that offer goods or services to EU people or monitor their behaviour. For AI that means a model trained or deployed anywhere can fall inside it if EU people are affected. Until the AI Act arrived the GDPR was the EU's main lever over AI, and it still applies alongside the Act rather than being replaced by it.

### The articles AI governance leans on

| Article | Rule |
|---|---|
| 5 | principles: lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity, accountability |
| 6 | six lawful bases, no hierarchy |
| 9 | special-category prohibition and exceptions |
| 13 to 15 | transparency and access, including automated-decision logic |
| 17 and 21 | erasure and objection, which reach profiling |
| 22 | solely automated decisions with legal or significant effects |
| 25 | privacy by design and by default |
| 28 | processor contracts |
| 33 and 34 | breach notification |
| 35 | DPIAs for high-risk processing |
| 44 to 49 | cross-border transfers |

### The AI pressure points

Article 22 bans solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects unless a contract, a law or explicit consent allows them, and even then requires safeguards including meaningful human intervention. Article 9 forbids processing special-category data unless a narrow exception applies, and AI can create that data by inference. Article 5(1)(b) purpose limitation blocks silent repurposing of data to train a model. Article 35 requires a DPIA for high-risk processing, which most consequential AI triggers.

### Penalties and status

Article 83 sets two tiers: up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover for many breaches, and up to EUR 20 million or 4% for the core principles and rights. The Commission's Digital Omnibus (COM(2025) 837, 19 November 2025) would amend the GDPR, but as of September 2026 those changes are proposals under negotiation, not law. Answer on the current text.
term:General Data Protection Regulation.exam_tip: The GDPR is the law that already reaches AI without naming it; the AI Act is the AI-specific layer on top, and both apply at once. Reach for Article 22 for automated decisions, Article 9 for special categories, Article 5(1)(b) for repurposed data, and Article 35 for DPIAs.

term:Data Controller.deep_dive:
A controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing (Article 4(7)); a processor acts on the controller's behalf (Article 4(8)). The accountability principle in Article 5(2) makes the controller responsible not only for complying but for being able to demonstrate compliance, and Article 24 adds responsibility for putting appropriate measures in place. Responsibilities cannot be delegated to a processor.

### The line that blurs in AI

In AI supply chains the controller and processor roles are harder to draw than in classic outsourcing. A cloud or model vendor that keeps training on customer data, or a black-box AI-as-a-service platform with little configuration, can become a joint controller. Article 28(10) states the rule plainly: a processor that determines the purposes and means of processing becomes a controller for that processing. A vendor that reuses customer data to improve its own models has crossed the line, whatever the contract says.

### Why the role matters for AI

The controller carries the duties AI questions test: a lawful basis under Article 6, the DPIA under Article 35, the processor contract under Article 28, transfer safeguards under Chapter V, answers to data subject rights, and the Article 22 safeguards for automated decisions. The CJEU's SCHUFA ruling (C-634/21, 7 December 2023) extends this outward: a credit bureau's automated score is itself an Article 22 decision where the lender draws strongly on it, so an upstream model or score provider can owe Article 22 duties, not only the business that acts on the output.

### Do not conflate the roles

The GDPR roles (controller, processor, joint controller) are not the AI Act roles (provider, deployer, importer, distributor). The same organization can be a controller under the GDPR and a deployer under the AI Act, or a processor and a provider. Read which statute the stem is applying before naming the role.
term:Data Controller.exam_tip: The controller determines purposes and means (Article 4(7)) and cannot delegate accountability (Article 5(2)). A processor that determines purposes becomes a controller (Article 28(10)), and SCHUFA shows an upstream score provider can owe Article 22 duties. Keep GDPR roles apart from AI Act roles.

term:Third-Party Processor.deep_dive:
A processor processes personal data on behalf of the controller (Article 4(8)). Article 28 governs the relationship: the controller may use only processors that give sufficient guarantees, and the processing must be governed by a binding contract, usually called a data processing agreement.

### What Article 28(3) requires

The contract must set out the subject matter, duration, nature and purpose of processing, the types of personal data and the categories of data subjects, and the processor's obligations: act only on documented instructions, keep confidentiality, secure the data under Article 32, follow the sub-processor rules, assist the controller with data subject rights and DPIAs, return or delete data at the end, allow audits, and tell the controller if an instruction would infringe the GDPR. Sub-processors need prior written authorisation, and the same duties flow down to them.

### Liability and the AI twist

Article 28(4) makes the initial processor fully liable if a sub-processor fails. Article 28(10) turns a processor that determines purposes and means into a controller. In AI, common processor relationships include cloud AI APIs, fine-tuning services, MLOps platforms and data labelling vendors. The recurring risk is processor drift: a vendor quietly trains on customer data, ships new features that change processing, or introduces profiling through a model update. Controllers should require notice of sub-processor changes, audit logs, and access to performance and fairness metrics.

### Due diligence for AI vendors

Ask whether the vendor uses subcontractors, can articulate training-data provenance, supports data subject requests, agrees to process only on instruction, and will accept an audit after a breach. A clause letting the vendor improve its own models with your data undercuts the controller's instructions and can breach purpose limitation.
term:Third-Party Processor.exam_tip: Article 28(3) lists what the processor contract must contain; Article 28(4) makes the processor liable for sub-processors, and Article 28(10) makes a processor that sets purposes a controller. In AI, watch processor drift: a vendor training on customer data has left the processor lane.

term:Data Protection Officer (DPO).deep_dive:
The DPO is a named role under Articles 37 to 39. Appointment is mandatory under Article 37(1) for a public authority or body (except courts acting in their judicial capacity), for organizations whose core activities involve regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale, and for those whose core activities involve large-scale processing of special-category data or data on criminal convictions and offences. The GDPR does not define large scale, so the assessment is contextual.

### Position and independence

The DPO must be involved properly and in time, report to the highest level of management, and be free from instructions on how to do the job. The DPO cannot be dismissed or penalized for performing it, must have no conflict of interest (so should not also hold a role that decides the purposes and means of processing), may be an external service provider, and must have contact details published and notified to the supervisory authority. The DPO is not personally liable; the controller remains accountable.

### Tasks (Article 39)

The DPO informs and advises the controller and staff, monitors compliance with the GDPR and internal policies, advises on and monitors the DPIA, cooperates with the supervisory authority, acts as its contact point, and works in a risk-based way.

### In AI governance

The DPO is the natural owner of AI privacy work: advising on the lawful basis and the legitimate-interest assessment, the Article 35 DPIA, and the privacy half of the AI Act's fundamental rights impact assessment. Note the distinction the exam tests: the DPO advises and monitors, but does not decide. The DPO is not the AI governance lead, and the two roles should not be merged in a fact pattern.
term:Data Protection Officer (DPO).exam_tip: Article 37(1) sets the three mandatory triggers, and Article 39 lists the tasks. The DPO advises and monitors but does not decide, cannot be instructed, must have no conflict of interest, and is not personally liable. Do not confuse the DPO with an AI governance lead.

term:Data Subject Rights.deep_dive:
The GDPR gives data subjects a bundle of rights in Articles 12 to 22: access (Article 15), rectification (Article 16), erasure (Article 17), restriction of processing (Article 18), data portability (Article 20), objection (Article 21), and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions (Article 22). Article 12 sets the mechanics: the controller must respond without undue delay and within one month, extendable by two further months for complex or numerous requests, generally free of charge.

### Why AI strains them

| Right | AI challenge |
|---|---|
| Access (15) | explaining a black-box output is hard |
| Rectification (16) | correcting data embedded in model weights |
| Erasure (17) | deleting a record from a trained model |
| Restriction (18) | halting use inside a continuously learning system |
| Portability (20) | outputs are model-dependent |
| Objection (21) | profiling is intrinsic to many AI systems |
| Automated decisions (22) | needs genuine human review |

The CJEU's Dun & Bradstreet Austria (C-203/22, 27 February 2025) defines what an access request about an automated decision must produce: a concise, intelligible account of the procedure and principles actually applied to that person's data. A formula or algorithm dump is not enough, and telling the person how different inputs would have changed the result may be. Claimed trade secrets go to the supervisory authority or court to balance, and a national rule excluding access as a rule is not allowed.

### Practical response

Design for rights from the start: build explainability and logging in, keep model metadata, use layered explanations, and plan deletion pipelines that exclude erased records from retraining. For sensitive data, confirm identity with extra caution and explain whether data was collected or inferred.
term:Data Subject Rights.exam_tip: Know the article for each right (15 access, 16 rectification, 17 erasure, 18 restriction, 20 portability, 21 objection, 22 automated decisions) and the Article 12 clock of one month. Dun & Bradstreet Austria is the case for what the explanation must contain.

term:Right to Erasure.deep_dive:
Article 17 gives the right to erasure, also called the right to be forgotten. The controller must erase personal data without undue delay where one of the listed grounds applies: the data is no longer necessary for the purpose, consent is withdrawn with no other basis, the person objects under Article 21(1) with no overriding grounds, the processing was unlawful, a legal obligation requires erasure, or the data was collected from a child in an information society service. Article 17(3) lists the exceptions: freedom of expression and information, a legal obligation, public health, archiving and research or statistics under Article 89(1), and legal claims. Where data was made public, Article 17(2) requires reasonable steps, including technical measures, to tell other controllers.

### Machine unlearning

Erasure is one of the hardest GDPR duties for AI. Deleting one person's data from a trained model is not the same as deleting a row from a database. Full retraining is expensive and often impractical for large models. Approximate unlearning methods, such as SISA training and gradient-based unlearning, are developing but are not yet proven for regulatory compliance. Differential privacy at training time reduces the influence of any single record, which makes later unlearning more feasible.

### Run the anonymity test first

Before assuming the model is out of scope, apply the EDPB Opinion 28/2024 test: a model is anonymous only if extracting a training subject's data from it, directly or through queries, is insignificantly likely. If it is not anonymous, the erasure request can reach the model, not just the training database. Embeddings in vector stores, and updates spread across federated learning, raise the same practical problem.

### The exam distinction

Erasure is not the same as anonymisation, and it is not absolute. If an Article 17(3) exception applies, the data need not be erased.
term:Right to Erasure.exam_tip: Article 17 has six grounds and five exceptions; the exceptions make erasure conditional, not absolute. For AI the issue is machine unlearning: retraining, approximate unlearning, differential privacy. Check the EDPB Opinion 28/2024 anonymity test before assuming the model is out of scope.

term:Purpose Limitation.deep_dive:
Purpose limitation, in Article 5(1)(b), requires personal data to be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a way incompatible with those purposes. It is one of the Article 5 principles and it is AI's chronic problem, because training is a tempting second use for data gathered for something else.

### Further processing and the compatibility test

Article 6(4) allows further processing that is not based on consent or a law if it is compatible with the original purpose. The assessment weighs the link between the purposes, the context of collection (including the relationship with the data subject), the nature of the data, the possible consequences of the further processing, and the safeguards in place. Further processing for archiving, scientific or historical research, or statistics under Article 89(1) is not treated as incompatible.

### How AI plays out

Purpose creep is the pattern: data collected to deliver a service is quietly reused to train a model, then reused again for a new feature. Three AI-specific pressures stand out. Training and inference can be different purposes. Licensed third-party models arrive trained on undisclosed datasets, so the downstream controller cannot see the original purpose. And users are rarely told the downstream purposes a model serves.

EDPB Opinion 28/2024 treats development and deployment as potentially separate purposes, so each needs its own assessment. The draft Guidelines 03/2026 push collection criteria to be precise, so a scraper does not hoover up data beyond the training purpose.

### Supporting the principle

Align dataset documentation with intended use, keep separate datasets for distinct tasks, run a compatibility assessment before any secondary use, and update the privacy notice at each material change.
term:Purpose Limitation.exam_tip: Article 5(1)(b) is the rule; Article 6(4) is the compatibility test for further processing, weighing links, context, data nature, consequences and safeguards. In AI, development and deployment may be separate purposes. Purpose creep and silent training reuse are the failures the exam describes.

term:Data Minimization.deep_dive:
Data minimisation, in Article 5(1)(c), requires personal data to be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the stated purpose. Article 25(2) reinforces it as data protection by default: only data necessary for each specific purpose is processed by default, covering the amount collected, the extent of processing, the storage period and accessibility.

### The AI tension

AI runs against minimisation. Model development wants large datasets, exploration is open-ended, and teams overcollect against a hypothetical future use. Minimisation is also a condition of the legitimate-interest test: under EDPB Opinion 28/2024, the necessity step asks whether no less intrusive route exists and whether the amount of personal data is proportionate to the purpose.

### Minimise at every stage

| Stage | Minimisation move |
|---|---|
| Collection | limit scope; avoid sensitive data unless strictly necessary; do not collect on speculation |
| Preprocessing | drop non-contributing features; mask or redact sensitive fields |
| Training | federated learning or differential privacy so raw personal data is not centralised |
| Inference | limit model input to the minimal feature set the task needs |

The framing to remember is smart data, not big data. Two levers do the work: collection discipline, which reduces scope and volume, and technical safeguards, which reduce identifiability. Techniques include masking and tokenization, pseudonymisation, on-device processing, homomorphic encryption, synthetic data, and differential privacy.

### The exam distinction

Minimisation is about necessity and proportionality, not about accuracy or storage duration. A system can minimise well and still be inaccurate; a system can keep data briefly and still overcollect. Read which principle the stem describes.
term:Data Minimization.exam_tip: Article 5(1)(c): adequate, relevant, limited to what is necessary. It is a condition of the legitimate-interest necessity step in EDPB Opinion 28/2024. Minimise across collection, preprocessing, training and inference, and keep it distinct from accuracy and storage limitation.

term:Pseudonymization.deep_dive:
Pseudonymisation, defined in Article 4(5), means processing personal data so that it can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information, provided that the additional information is kept separately and is subject to technical and organisational measures that prevent attribution. The crucial point: pseudonymised data is still personal data. Removing a name is pseudonymisation, not anonymisation, so the GDPR continues to apply.

### Where the GDPR calls for it

Article 25(1) names pseudonymisation as an appropriate technical measure for data protection by design. Article 32(1)(a) names it among security measures. Article 89(1) links it to safeguards for archiving, research and statistics. Recital 26 distinguishes it from anonymous information. Because the data stays in scope, lawful basis, purpose limitation and data subject rights all still apply.

### The AI angle

For AI, pseudonymisation is a way to reduce identifiability without giving up the dataset. EDPB Opinion 28/2024 lists reducing identifiability as one of the evidence areas for an anonymity claim, and the EU AI Act's Article 4a safeguards (added by the AI Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) include re-use limits and pseudonymisation when special-category data is used strictly for bias detection and correction.

### The distinction the exam tests

Pseudonymisation is reversible with the key, so the data remains personal and in scope. Anonymisation is irreversible, so the GDPR no longer applies. A proposal in the Digital Omnibus (COM(2025) 837) would define when pseudonymised data stops being personal data by implementing act; the EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 2/2026 opposes that approach, and the change is not law.
term:Pseudonymization.exam_tip: Pseudonymised data is still personal data (Article 4(5)): the key exists, so the GDPR still applies. That is the whole difference from anonymisation. Article 25 names it as a by-design safeguard, and the AI Act's Article 4a includes it for bias-detection processing.

term:Anonymization.deep_dive:
Anonymisation removes the link between data and a person so completely that the GDPR no longer applies. Article 4(1) defines personal data by reference to an identified or identifiable natural person, and recital 26 says the principles of data protection do not apply to anonymous information, meaning information that does not relate to an identified or identifiable natural person or to data rendered anonymous so that the subject is no longer identifiable. Identifiability considers all the means reasonably likely to be used, including singling out.

### The model question

A trained model is not automatically anonymous. Under EDPB Opinion 28/2024, a model is anonymous only if both likelihoods are insignificant: direct or probabilistic extraction of training subjects' data from the model, and obtaining that data through queries. The controller documents how it limited collection, reduced identifiability, prevented extraction, and tested resistance to state-of-the-art attacks. If the model is not anonymous, lawful basis, rights and security duties reach the model itself.

### Three tests

Draft EDPB Guidelines 02/2026 propose three tests: no record isolation, no linkage, and no inference. Anonymity can differ from one holder to another, following the CJEU's EDPS v SRB (C-413/23 P, 4 September 2025).

### The exam distinction

Pseudonymisation is reversible and stays in scope. Anonymisation is irreversible and takes the data out of scope. Aggregation alone is not anonymisation, and re-identification by combination is always possible in principle, so the bar is high.
term:Anonymization.exam_tip: Anonymisation takes data out of GDPR scope; pseudonymisation does not. For AI models, apply the EDPB Opinion 28/2024 test: anonymous only if extraction and query-based recovery are both insignificantly likely. The draft Guidelines 02/2026 three tests are no isolation, no linkage, no inference.

term:Personally Identifiable Information.deep_dive:
PII is the United States framing. NIST Special Publication 800-122 defines personally identifiable information as any information that can be used to distinguish or trace an individual's identity, either alone or when combined with other information that is linked or linkable to a specific individual. That definition is the one US privacy and security law tends to use, and the FTC treats failures around PII under its section 5 authority over unfair or deceptive practices.

### How it compares with personal data

The GDPR's term is personal data, defined in Article 4(1) as any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person. The EU concept is broader in a way that matters for AI: identifiability reaches anyone who can be singled out, directly or indirectly, and recital 30 confirms that online identifiers such as IP addresses and cookie identifiers can be personal data. A pseudonymous identifier, a device ID or a location trace is personal data under the GDPR even where a US analysis might not call it PII.

### Why the distinction matters

Three AI consequences follow. Training corpora usually contain personal data, so the GDPR's rules attach before any model is trained. Inferred attributes are personal data too, because they relate to an identifiable person, which is how Article 9 can apply to a health prediction built from purchase history. And synthetic or aggregated data needs care, because neither is automatically anonymous.

### The exam distinction

The test is relation to an identifiable person, not the label on a field. Read whether the stem uses the US term PII or the EU term personal data, and apply the wider EU standard when the GDPR is in play.
term:Personally Identifiable Information.exam_tip: PII is the US framing (NIST SP 800-122: distinguish or trace an identity); personal data is the EU framing (Article 4(1)) and is broader, reaching indirect identifiability and online identifiers. Inferred attributes are personal data, so Article 9 can apply to what was never collected.

term:Special Category Data.deep_dive:
Article 9(1) prohibits processing of special-category data unless a narrow exception applies. The categories are racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person, data concerning health, and data concerning a person's sex life or sexual orientation. Article 9(2) lists the exceptions, with explicit consent the usual one, alongside employment and social protection law, vital interests, not-for-profit bodies, data manifestly made public by the subject, legal claims, substantial public interest, preventive and occupational medicine, public health, and archiving or research under Article 89(1). Article 9(4) lets member states add conditions for genetic, biometric and health data.

### AI meets sensitive data three ways

Deliberate use (a health tool reading medical records), incidental collection (a CV sorter harvesting political affiliation from past activism), and inferential collection, where a model predicts ethnicity, health or orientation without ever being told it. Supervisory authorities increasingly treat inferred special-category data as falling inside Article 9(1).

### Two locks, not one

Draft EDPB Guidelines 03/2026 make the point for scraping: processing special-category data needs both an Article 6 lawful basis and an Article 9(2) exception. The EU AI Act's Article 4a, added by the AI Omnibus (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744), gives an AI Act basis to process special-category data strictly for bias detection and correction, with six safeguards and the GDPR conditions applying in addition.

### Jurisdictional edges

The CPRA adds precise geolocation; Brazil's LGPD, Canada's PIPEDA and India's DPDP Act track similar lists.
term:Special Category Data.exam_tip: Article 9 is a prohibition, not a consent requirement: processing is banned unless an Article 9(2) exception applies. Inferred sensitive data counts. For scraping, sensitive data needs both an Article 6 basis and an Article 9(2) exception. Explicit consent is the usual route, not the only one.

term:Article 9 GDPR.deep_dive:
Article 9 is the GDPR's rule for special categories of personal data. It works differently from the other articles, and that difference is what the exam tests. Article 9(1) starts from a prohibition: processing of the listed categories is forbidden. Article 9(2) then lists the conditions under which the prohibition does not apply. So the question is never which lawful basis to pick in the abstract; it is whether a specific Article 9(2) exception is available.

### The prohibition and the exceptions

The prohibited categories are racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data used to uniquely identify a person, health data, and sex life or sexual orientation. The Article 9(2) exceptions include explicit consent, employment and social protection law, vital interests where the subject cannot consent, not-for-profit bodies, data manifestly made public by the subject, legal claims, substantial public interest, preventive and occupational medicine, public health, and archiving or research with safeguards.

### Article 6 and Article 9 together

Sensitive data needs both. Article 6 supplies the lawful basis for the processing, and Article 9(2) lifts the prohibition on this category. Consent and contract are not interchangeable here: sensitive data under Article 9(2)(a) needs explicit, revocable consent, while contract necessity is a demanding test that nice-to-have features fail. Article 22(4) adds a further limit: automated decisions must not be based on Article 9(1) data unless Article 9(2)(a) or (g) applies and suitable safeguards are in place.

### The AI hook

AI creates Article 9 data by inference, so a model that predicts health or ethnicity from ordinary inputs is processing special-category data even though nobody collected a special-category field.
term:Article 9 GDPR.exam_tip: Article 9 is a default prohibition with exceptions, not a basis-selection menu. Sensitive data needs an Article 6 basis and an Article 9(2) exception together. Explicit consent is the common route. Inferred sensitive data falls inside Article 9(1), and Article 22(4) limits automated decisions on it.

term:Article 22 GDPR.deep_dive:
Article 22 is the GDPR's automated decision-making rule and, for AI, its most consequential provision. Article 22(1) gives a person the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them. The word that does the work is solely. If a human is genuinely involved, Article 22 does not bite.

### Exceptions and safeguards

Article 22(2) allows such decisions where they are necessary for a contract, authorised by Union or member state law with safeguards, or based on the subject's explicit consent. Where a contract or explicit consent is the route, Article 22(3) requires safeguards: the right to obtain human intervention, to express a point of view, and to contest the decision. Article 22(4) forbids automated decisions based on Article 9(1) special-category data unless Article 9(2)(a) or (g) applies and safeguards are in place.

### What counts as meaningful human involvement

Human review must be real, not a rubber stamp. The reviewer needs authority and competence to change the decision and must consider all the relevant data. A person clicking approve on an AI recommendation does not satisfy the requirement. The CJEU's SCHUFA (C-634/21, 7 December 2023) extends the reach: a credit bureau's automated probability value is itself an Article 22 decision where the lender draws strongly on it, so an upstream score provider owes Article 22 duties.

### The explanation

Dun & Bradstreet Austria (C-203/22, 27 February 2025) defines the Article 15(1)(h) explanation for such decisions: an intelligible account of the procedure and principles actually applied. The EU AI Act's Article 14 human oversight duty builds on this for high-risk systems.
term:Article 22 GDPR.exam_tip: The hinge is solely: no human, or a rubber-stamp human, triggers Article 22. Cite the three exceptions (contract, law, explicit consent) and the three safeguards (human intervention, express a view, contest). SCHUFA pulls upstream score providers in, and Article 14 of the AI Act builds on it.

term:Article 35 GDPR.deep_dive:
Article 35 requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment where a type of processing, in particular using new technologies, is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. The reference to new technologies is what pulls AI inside it. The DPIA is a process, not a document: describe the processing, assess necessity and proportionality, assess the risks, and record the measures that address them.

### The three mandatory triggers

Article 35(3) makes a DPIA mandatory for: systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing, including profiling, on which decisions are based that produce legal effects or similarly significantly affect the subject; large-scale processing of Article 9 special-category data or Article 10 criminal-conviction data; and systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale. Supervisory authorities publish lists of processing that needs a DPIA under Article 35(4).

### What the DPIA must contain (Article 35(7))

A systematic description of the processing and its purposes, an assessment of necessity and proportionality, an assessment of the risks to rights and freedoms, and the measures to address those risks, including safeguards and security. Article 35(9) says the controller should seek the views of data subjects where appropriate. If residual high risk remains after mitigation, Article 36 requires prior consultation with the supervisory authority.

### AI practice

Most consequential AI triggers Article 35(3)(a). The common pitfalls are unclear system boundaries between model and business logic, framing technical risk instead of human impact, and never revisiting the DPIA once a model keeps learning. The EU AI Act's Article 27 fundamental rights impact assessment for certain high-risk deployers overlaps and can be coordinated.
term:Article 35 GDPR.exam_tip: Article 35(1) is the general test (new technologies, likely high risk); Article 35(3) gives the three mandatory triggers; Article 35(7) lists the required content. In AI, profiling with significant effects is the usual trigger. Article 36 prior consultation follows if residual risk stays high.

term:Breach Notification.deep_dive:
Article 33 requires a controller to notify the competent supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay and, where feasible, no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to rights and freedoms. Where notification is late, it must be accompanied by reasons for the delay. Article 33(3) sets the content: the nature of the breach including the categories and approximate number of data subjects and records concerned, the DPO or other contact point, the likely consequences, and the measures taken or proposed. Article 33(5) requires the controller to document all breaches, whether or not they are notified. A processor must notify the controller without undue delay under Article 33(2).

### Telling the individuals

Article 34 requires communication to the data subjects without undue delay where the breach is likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms, in clear and plain language, with the same kind of content. Article 34(3) lists exceptions where the controller had applied measures that make the data unintelligible (such as encryption), where later measures removed the high risk, or where individual communication would involve disproportionate effort, in which case a public communication is used instead.

### The AI-specific vectors

AI adds breach types that classic data-loss prevention does not watch: training-data leakage through inversion, membership inference or gradient extraction; output leakage where a model reproduces training data or a prompt injection exposes content; bias amplification that harms at scale; and model drift or poisoning. Detection is harder because failures can be silent and pipelines are opaque. Penalties sit in the lower Article 83 tier, up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global turnover. The Digital Omnibus proposal would raise the threshold and extend the deadline to 96 hours, but it is not law.
term:Breach Notification.exam_tip: 72 hours to the supervisory authority (Article 33), no undue delay to individuals for high-risk breaches (Article 34), and document every breach (Article 33(5)). Know the Article 34(3) exceptions. For AI, watch training-data leakage, output leakage and prompt injection as the distinct vectors.

term:Cross-Border Data Transfer.deep_dive:
Chapter V of the GDPR, Articles 44 to 49, governs transfers of personal data outside the EU and EEA. Article 44 sets the principle: a transfer is allowed only if the conditions in the chapter are met, so that the level of protection guaranteed by the GDPR is not undermined, and the rule covers onward transfers too. Access from outside the EEA counts as a transfer even if no data is stored there.

### The mechanisms

Article 45 allows transfer to a country the Commission has decided ensures an adequate level of protection, with no specific authorisation needed; adequacy decisions are reviewed at least every four years. Japan, South Korea, the UK and the US (under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework) hold adequacy. In the absence of adequacy, Article 46 allows transfer with appropriate safeguards and enforceable rights, including standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules under Article 47, approved codes of conduct, and approved certification mechanisms. Article 48 says third-country court or administrative orders are enforceable only under an international agreement such as a mutual legal assistance treaty. Article 49 gives derogations for specific situations, including explicit consent and legal claims, with a narrow last-resort route for compelling legitimate interests.

### Schrems II and transfer impact assessments

The CJEU's Schrems II (C-311/18, 16 July 2020) invalidated the EU-US Privacy Shield and held that standard contractual clauses require a case-by-case assessment of the destination country. A transfer impact assessment examines the destination's laws and government access, the nature of the data and processing, and supplementary measures such as encryption and pseudonymisation.

### The AI angle

Global AI infrastructure triggers all of this: cloud training and inference on non-EEA infrastructure, offshore model training with EU data, US-based LLM APIs, and remote inference calls that pull personal data across borders.
term:Cross-Border Data Transfer.exam_tip: Chapter V is a ladder: adequacy (Article 45), then safeguards (Article 46, including SCCs and BCRs), then derogations (Article 49). Access from outside the EEA is a transfer. Schrems II made transfer impact assessments necessary for SCCs and BCRs. US-based AI APIs and offshore training are the common AI patterns.

term:Biometric Data.deep_dive:
Article 4(14) defines biometric data as personal data resulting from specific technical processing relating to the physical, physiological or behavioural characteristics of a natural person, which allow or confirm the unique identification of that person, such as facial images or dactyloscopic data. Article 9(1) makes it a special category only when it is processed for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person. That purpose test is the hinge the exam tests.

### The identification line

Biometric data used to identify or verify a person is special-category data and needs an Article 9(2) exception, with explicit consent the usual route. Biometric categorisation that does not link an image to an identity, such as age estimation, may fall outside Article 9, but it still carries risk and can trigger other rules. Biometric data is especially sensitive because, unlike a password or a card number, it cannot be changed if it is compromised.

### Common types and AI uses

Facial features, fingerprints, iris and retina, voiceprints, gait and typing rhythm. AI uses them for authentication, identification, emotion detection and surveillance analytics. The three ways AI meets sensitive data apply here: deliberate use, incidental collection, and inference, where a model predicts a trait without being told it.

### The EU AI Act overlay

The AI Act prohibits several biometric practices in Article 5(1): untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases; biometric categorisation by sensitive traits; and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces, with narrow law-enforcement exceptions. Emotion recognition in workplaces and education is also prohibited, and deployers of permitted emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems owe transparency duties. The GDPR and the AI Act apply together.
term:Biometric Data.exam_tip: Article 4(14) defines biometric data; Article 9(1) makes it special-category only when used to uniquely identify. Identification is the line, so categorisation may fall outside Article 9 but still carries risk. Overlay the AI Act's Article 5(1) bans on facial scraping, sensitive-trait categorisation and real-time public identification.

term:EDPB Opinion 28/2024.deep_dive:
The EDPB adopted Opinion 28/2024 on 17 December 2024 under Article 64(2), at the request of the Irish supervisory authority. It addresses how the GDPR applies to AI models and answers four questions: when a model is anonymous, how to rely on legitimate interest in development, how to rely on it in deployment, and what unlawful development means for later use.

### The anonymity test

A model trained on personal data cannot be assumed anonymous. It is anonymous only if both likelihoods are insignificant, taking account of all means reasonably likely to be used: direct or probabilistic extraction of training subjects' data from the model, and obtaining such data, intentionally or not, through queries. The controller documents how it limited collection, reduced identifiability, prevented extraction, and tested resistance to state-of-the-art attacks. If the model is not anonymous, lawful basis, rights and security duties reach the model itself.

### The three-step legitimate-interest test

First, the interest must be lawful, clearly articulated, and real and present, not speculative. Second, necessity: the processing must actually achieve the interest, with no less intrusive route and a proportionate amount of data. Third, balancing: the interest must not be overridden by the data subjects' interests, rights and freedoms, with reasonable expectations carrying weight. Mitigating measures count only if they go beyond what the GDPR already requires. There is no hierarchy among the Article 6 bases.

### Unlawful development

The Opinion covers three scenarios: the same controller deploys a model holding personal data (case by case); a different controller deploys it (that deployer must assess, as part of accountability, that the model was not developed unlawfully); and a model developed unlawfully then genuinely anonymised (the earlier unlawfulness does not taint the anonymous operation). The press shorthand is that unlawful training can affect deployment unless the model has been duly anonymised.
term:EDPB Opinion 28/2024.exam_tip: Opinion 28/2024 gives three things to cite: the model anonymity test (extraction and query-based recovery both insignificantly likely), the three-step legitimate-interest test (interest, necessity, balancing), and the three unlawful-development scenarios. It guides case-by-case assessment, it is not a pre-approval.

term:EDPB Guidelines 03/2026 on Web Scra.deep_dive:
The EDPB adopted draft Guidelines 03/2026 on 7 July 2026 as version 1.0, open for public consultation until 30 October 2026. They cover private entities that scrape internet sources, directly or through contractors, to train generative AI. The status matters: these are draft guidelines for consultation, not final, so a stem that treats them as binding is wrong.

### Scope and roles

The GDPR applies whenever scraping involves personal data, covering collection, storage, organisation and retrieval. The roles of controller, joint controller and processor are assessed case by case, so a scraping contractor is not automatically a processor.

### Lawful basis

Consent would most probably not be an applicable basis for large-scale indirect collection. Legitimate interest is the basis often used, and it must pass the three cumulative conditions from Opinion 28/2024: a real and present interest, necessity with no less intrusive route and proportionate data, and a balancing test where reasonable expectations weigh heavily.

### The practical conditions the guidelines set

Transparency: individual notices may be unnecessary where it is impossible or disproportionate under Article 14(5)(b), depending on design. Minimisation: consider synthetic data first, set precise collection criteria, filter out categories of data, exclude sites that structurally hold sensitive data or clearly object to scraping, and pseudonymise, anonymise or delete early. Accuracy: scrape from reliable sources, timestamp, and validate before training.

### Two locks for sensitive data

Scraping that processes special-category data needs both an Article 6 lawful basis and an Article 9(2) exception. There is no general exemption, and the guidelines suggest the CJEU's GC and Others reasoning may cover incidental and residual collection only where the controller has measures to prevent collection and dissemination.
term:EDPB Guidelines 03/2026 on Web Scra.exam_tip: Guidelines 03/2026 are a draft (adopted 7 July 2026, consultation to 30 October 2026). Consent is rarely workable for large-scale scraping; legitimate interest is the usual basis, passing the Opinion 28/2024 three-step test. Sensitive data needs both an Article 6 basis and an Article 9(2) exception.

term:Valid and Reliable.deep_dive:
**Valid and reliable** is first among NIST's seven trustworthiness characteristics, and the framework calls it the necessary foundation: a system that does not work as intended cannot be trustworthy in any other respect. The two words are not synonyms. **Valid** means the system meets the requirements for its intended use, so it is accurate for the task it was built for. **Reliable** means it produces consistent results over repeated runs and over time, under the conditions it was designed for.

NIST folds accuracy, robustness and reliability together under this heading, and MEASURE 2.5 is where the exam usually lands: the AI system to be deployed is demonstrated to be valid and reliable, and limitations on generalizability beyond the development conditions are documented. That last clause matters. A model shown to work on one population, language or time period is not automatically valid elsewhere, and the gap must be written down, not assumed away.

The distinction the exam tests is scope. Validity is about correctness for the intended use, reliability is about consistency, and both are measured only against **specified conditions**. Change the conditions and the demonstration no longer holds. Generative AI stretches both at once, because the same prompt can yield different outputs (weak reliability) and fluent text can be confidently wrong (invalid).
term:Valid and Reliable.exam_tip: Valid means correct for the intended use; reliable means consistent across runs and time. Both are conditional on the specified conditions, so changing context breaks the demonstration. MEASURE 2.5 is the subcategory that tests this.
